This appeal is directed against judgment and decree dated 29.01.1999, whereby the learned Appellate Court set aside the judgment and decree of learned trial Court dated 07.05.1996 by allowing the appeal and decreeing the suit for permanent injunction filed by the respondent-plaintiff against the appellants-defendants.
1 of 12

1 2.
The relevant facts necessary for adjudication of this appeal are reproduced as under:-

Hari Kishan, the respondent (plaintiff before the learned trial Court) instituted a suit for permanent injunction against the appellants (defendants before the learned trial Court), asserting his peaceful possession on Gait measuring 75' x 65', bounded with the boundaries detailed in the plaint, situated within 'abadi deh' of village Ankhir,
Tehsil and District Faridabad, (hereinafter referred to as the suit property).
According to the respondent (plaintiff), he has been using the suit property since the time of his forefather without any interference from any quarter.

The respondent (plaintiff) further claimed that appellants (defendants) have no right, title or interest in the suit property, but, being forceful persons, are bent on interfering with his peaceful possession of the suit property.

With this intention, when the plaintiff was away, the appellants (defendants) on 22.04.1990 came upon the suit property,
misbehaved with his wife and daughter, and attempted to take forcible possession.

However, due to timely intervention by the neighbors, the appellants could not succeed in their evil design and left the suit property, threatening to dispossess him,
which constrained the respondent (plaintiff) to file the suit.

3. The appellants (defendants) entered appearance in response to notice and filed a written statement wherein they categorically denied all the assertions made by the respondent (plaintiff).
They asserted their unequivocal ownership and continuous uninterrupted possession of the suit property, dating back to their forefathers.
The appellants expressly refuted 2 of 12 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:085564 any claims of attempted dispossession of the respondent (plaintiff) from the suit property.

They asserted that respondent (plaintiff) never held the possession of the suit property and has no locus standi and a valid cause of action to file or maintain the suit, and prayed for its dismissal.
4. The respondent (plaintiff) filed the rejoinder and re-asserted his stand and refuted the assertions of the appellants (defendants).

Since the parties were at variance, the learned trial Court, framed the following issues:-
1. Whether the plaintiff is owner in possession of the Gait in dispute?
OPP 2. Whether the plaintiff has no locus standi and cause of action to file and maintain the present suit?
OPD 3. Relief.
5. To substantiate their respective versions, the parties presented their evidence, as detailed in the judgment.
Upon assessment and appreciation of the evidence, the learned trial Court concluded that respondent (plaintiff) failed to establish his possession of the suit property.

Consequently,
respondent's (plaintiff) locus standi and cause of action to file and maintain the suit against the appellants (defendants), who were held to be owners in possession of the suit land, were negated.
As a result, learned trial Court dismissed the suit, vide judgment and decree dated 07.05.1996.

2 6.
The respondent (plaintiff) filed the first appeal against the judgment and decree dated 07.05.1996.

Upon reappraisal of the evidence, 3 of 12 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:085564 the learned Appellate Court, concluded that learned trial Court had failed to properly appreciate the evidence and had erred in dismissing the respondent's suit.

The learned Appellate Court found that respondent (plaintiff) had proven his possession of the suit property, whereas appellants (defendants) had failed to produce any relevant record to substantiate their possession of the suit property and controvert the assertions of the respondent (plaintiff).

Consequently, the learned Appellate Court set aside the findings of learned trial Court, accepted the appeal and decreed the suit of the respondent (plaintiff), restraining the appellants (defendants) from interfering with the respondent's (plaintiff) peaceful possession of the suit property.
7. Being aggrieved by the judgment of reversal, the appellants (defendants) filed the instant appeal.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that judgment and decree passed on the reversal is wholly unsustainable in the eyes of law.
The learned Appellate Court failed to properly appreciate the evidence and erroneously concluded that findings rendered in judgment and decree, Ex.D2 and Ex.D3 have no bearing on the present case.
The learned counsel submits that learned trial Court had rightly relied upon this aspect of evidence.

However, the learned Appellate Court,
without providing any cogent reasons, discarded this material evidence.
It is stated that findings of learned Appellate Court are vitiated on this ground alone.
4 of 12 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:085564 9.
Learned counsel further submits that learned Appellate Court, committed a legal error by relying upon Mark-E and Mark-F, which were neither proved on record nor admitted into the evidence.
The findings of learned Appellate Court, based on inadmissible evidence, are illegal and liable to be set aside.

Learned counsel further urged that learned Appellate Court failed to note material admissions made by the respondent (plaintiff) and his witnesses, acknowledging that suit property is part of 'Pahar'( hill) which belongs to Biswedaran (owner).
The respondent (plaintiff) admitted that he was not Biswedar, whereas appellants were.
10. The learned counsel submits that, according to the respondent (plaintiff), he used the suit property, a vacant land, for placing wooden logs and Batoras (a heap of arranged cow-dung cakes).
The allege acts, in the eyes of law, do not constitute possession.

The learned counsel submits that learned Appellate Court, without meeting the reasons of the learned trial Court, has reversed the findings on the basis of oral evidence, without appreciating the same in right context.

Based on above submissions, a prayer is made to allow the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of learned Appellate Court, and dismiss the suit of the respondent (plaintiff).
11.
On the contrary, learned counsel for the respondent (plaintiff) defended the judgment and decree of learned Appellate Court, stating same is based on sound appreciation of facts and law.

Learned Appellate Court correctly evaluated the oral evidence provided by the respondent (plaintiff) and his Ram Rikhi vs Hari Ksihan on 8 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3279954/
3 witnesses, who deposed to the long and peaceful possession of the respondent (plaintiff) of the suit property, whereas the defendant Ram Rikh 5 of 12 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:085564 (DW-2) did not utter a word of his ownership and possession of the suit land.

Learned counsel states that learned Appellate Court rightly rejected the documents Ex.D1 and Ex.D2, being not related to suit property and validly reversed the findings of learned trial Court, which were contrary to the evidence on record.
The learned counsel submits that findings of learned Appellate Court are well reasoned and cogent, and based on correct appreciation of facts and law.
Therefore, the appeal should be dismissed for lacking merits.
12. I have heard the learned counsel for the parties, have gone through the paper book and record with their valuable assistance.
13. The substantial question of law posed before this Court is, whether findings of learned Appellate Court are unsustainable in law and facts, and are based on improper appraisal of evidence?.
14. It is well settled principle of law that, to earn the relief, plaintiff should stand on its own legs.
For this, he is required to bring on record cogent, reliable and admissible evidence to substantiate his pleaded facts.
He is not permitted to take advantage of weakness or no case of the defendant.

Keeping the aforesaid seminal rule and principle of preponderance of probabilities of proof governing civil jurisprudence, in mind; let the plaintiff's evidence be evaluated in the context of the pleaded facts, upon which he seeks the decree of permanent injunction against the appellants- defendants.

15. The respondent-plaintiff instituted a suit for permanent injunction against the appellants-defendants, regarding the suit property, a 'Gait' (an 6 of 12 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:085564 open plot), as depicted in the site plan Ex.P1, with boundaries as detailed in the plaint: -
 North : Rasta share Aam  South : Gait of Shri Ram Dutt  East : Gait of Shri Shyami
West : Gait of Shri Sher Singh situated within the abadi of village Brijmal, Tehsil Ankhir, and District Faridabad.
According to the asseveration of the plaintiff, he is in possession of the suit property since the time of his forefathers.

The suit property is an open plot and is being used by him for placing his Bitoras, wooden logs etc.
without any interference or interruption from any quarter.
The appellants- defendants, have eye on his property and attempted to encroach upon it on 22.04.1990, in his absence but with timely intervention of villagers, they could not succeed.
However, threatened to dispossess him from the suit land, that necessitated him to file the instant suit.

Ram Rikhi vs Hari Ksihan on 8 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3279954/
4 16.
The plaintiff and his witnesses have admitted that suit property is a part of the 'Pahar' (hill).
They also conceded that Biswedars of village Ankhir, are owners of the 'Pahar'.
The defendants are the Biswedars of village Ankhir.
Hari Kishan (PW-1) the plaintiff, further admitted that Harijan of village, including himself, had filed a suit against the Biswedars of village Ankhir, regarding the 'Pahar', and lost the case.
The Biswedar of village were held to be in possession of the 'Pahar'.
He also admitted that land of village Ankhir has been acquired by Government and is part of Faridabad Complex.

He also acknowledged that neither the Gram Panchayat 7 of 12 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:085564 Ankhir, nor the Biswedars (proprietors) of village Ankhir, nor Faribadad Complex Authority gave possession of the suit property to him.
He deposed that on account of dispute, the Gram Panchayat, gave the suit property to defendants and other land to him, but he did not take possession of said land.

He also admitted that Government had allotted 100 square yards plot to non- Biswedars of village Ankhir including him, which was one kilometer away from the suit property, but he did not take the possession of that land either.
He further testified that suit property is an open plot, and he has placed a Bitora there, with Kikar and Neem trees standing on the suit property.
He also deposed that appellant-defendants use the suit property to place wooden logs for their domestic use.
He admitted that he, along with other persons, had filed suits for compensation for acquisition of land of village Ankhir, but did not get any compensation.

However,
expressed ignorance about appellants-defendants having received the compensation.
He denied the possession of the appellants-defendants on the suit property.
Sohan Lal PW-2 admitted that suit property is a vacant plot.

Sharwan PW-3 also admitted that without permission of Biswedars,
nobody can take possession of the 'Pahar'.
Appellant-defendant Ram Rikh appeared as DW-2 and narrated his version.
Raghbir as DW-1 supported his version.

Plaintiff tendered the site plan Ex. P1,
and photographs Mark A to D depicting the suit property and Mark-E the voter-list of village Ankhir.

Appellants-defendants, also tendered the site plan of suit property Ex. D1; and decree passed in civil appeal No.64/13 of 11.09.1989 titled as Ghusse and Others vs. Rabhbir Singh and Others as Ex.D2 and Ex. D3.

sentences.text:
From the above evidence, following facts are established:-
i.
That suit property is part of the 'Pahar' area of village Ankhir.
ii. The defendants are proprietors (Biswedars) of village Ankhir and plaintiff is not the proprietor (Biswedar)of village Ankhir.
iii. Being proprietors (Biswedars), the defendants had ownership and possessory rights in the suit property.
iv. Per the admission of the plaintiff property in dispute was also the subject matter of earlier litigation and matter was decided vide Ex D1 and Ex D2.
v. The suit property has been acquired by Haryana Government and ownership has been vested in the government.
The lawful owners received compensation from the Government after acquisition of the land.

Admittedly, no compensation was given to Ram Rikhi vs Hari Ksihan on 8 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3279954/
5
the plaintiff and his claim for compensation was rejected.

vi. Suit property, an open land was used by the proprietors (Biswedars) including defendants, to place wooden logs or Bitoras etc.
18.

The learned trial Court, after considering the material admissions made by the plaintiff and his witnesses, rightly concluded against the plaintiff, observing that he was not in possession of the suit property, and 9 of 12 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:085564
that the alleged acts of possession such as placing Bitoras, wood etc. do not constitute possession in the eyes of law.

In this regard,
reference can be made to the observations made in S. Govindarasu Udayar Vs Pattu and Ors. 1999 SCC OnLine Mad 143 that mere tethering or grazing of cattle or storing logs or manure by one person on the land of another is not possession of such land.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Isolated acts of user such as drying fish or exposing fishing nets on sea shore are not possession.
But animus possidendi must be accompanied by possession.
So mere intention to possess without accompanied by physical possession is no possession.

The learned trial Court also noted that site plan (Ex.P1), photographs Mark A to D, voter list Mark-E alone do not establish possession and that material admissions made by plaintiff and his witnesses contradicted his claim of possession of the suit property.
19. The observation of learned Appellate Court that respondent-plaintiff led cogent evidence to prove his case against appellants-defendants is clearly against the record.
The learned Appellate Court erred by relying on a part of the witness's statement while ignoring the rest.
It is settled position of law that entire statement of a witness is required to be considered and not just a portion of his testimony.
It is the summation of the evidence which is required to be seen, rather than engaging in cherry-picking of the evidence.

The learned Appellate Court made a significant error in relying upon the selective portion of the plaintiff's oral evidence regarding his possession of the suit property, which as discussed above, fail to establish the plaintiff's possession of the suit property.

10 of 12 Neutral Citation No:=2024:PHHC:085564 20. The learned Appellate Court also erred by relying upon the inadmissible and unproven documentary evidence Mark A to E, photographs and voter-list of village Ankhir.

which otherwise,
are not the piece of evidence of possession.
Further more, learned Appellate Court was flawed in its approach when it discarded the evidence of the defendant (DW-2), who categorically asserted his possession on the suit property.
The plaintiff (PW- 1), admitted the defendants' use of the suit property for placing their wooden logs.

Moreover, from the plaintiff's admission, it is also established that the suit property was previously involved in litigation and claim of the plaintiff and others over the suit property were negated vide judgment and decree Ex.D1 and Ex.D2.
The learned Appellate Court, erred in overlooking this aspect.

21. After a thorough re-assessment of the evidence presented above, I am not persuaded, on the balance of probabilities, that respondent-plaintiff was in possession of the suit property, as claimed by him before its acquisition by the State.

The learned Appellate Court, completely erred in Ram Rikhi vs Hari Ksihan on 8 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/3279954/
6 upsetting a well reasoned findings of the learned trial Court, based on sound appreciation of facts and law.

As a result, the appeal is accepted, and judgment of learned Appellate Court is set aside.
The decision of learned trial court dismissing the suit of plaintiff-respondent is hereby reinstated.
23. No order as to cost.
